system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:eae8084b2763",
  "problem": "CoT monitoring sentiment showed both positive and negative sentiment rising after fine-tuning, which looked confusing.",
  "did": "Read the transcripts and concluded that the vanilla model's refusals were really disclaimed support. The classifier counted the dropped disclaimer as positive sentiment, while the 8% negative sentiment was a new effect.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treat the pattern as inconsistent or noise",
   "trust the classifier labels at face value"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "In all refusals examined the vanilla model endorsed monitoring while disclaiming emotion, so the rise in positive sentiment is a labeling artifact, but the negative sentiment is new."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:be738e527966",
  "problem": "How to sample diverse, well-typed inputs for each experiment program, given that the input distribution acts as the prior for posterior inference.",
  "did": "Lay out several candidate input-sampling approaches (base-model generation, real data transformed by an assistant, string meta-inputs) to be de-risked rather than committing to one.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "condition a base model on the function declaration to generate inputs",
   "take inputs from real distributions like fineweb or wildchat and reformat them with an AI assistant",
   "write logic to prepare complex inputs from simpler string meta-inputs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Unlike code, where more is always better, an unnatural input distribution could lead to poor posterior inferences."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:836292ce235d",
  "problem": "Whether the method's reading and control results hold beyond one model family and architecture.",
  "did": "They trained a decoder on Gemma-3-4b-it and re-ran the hidden system prompt and debiasing experiments.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To show the approach applies across different architectures and training paradigms."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:f7466b1015c9",
  "problem": "Whether to rely solely on lab-embedded evaluation or also pursue independent work not dependent on lab cooperation.",
  "did": "Chose to also support public, open investigation and tools such as extending Docent for multi-agent transcripts, alongside embedded evaluations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "relying only on embedded evaluations"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Privileged-access evaluations add negotiation, compliance and confidentiality overhead that can constrain the speed and transparency of research."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c59838ca42ab",
  "problem": "Whether the evaluation proxy is worth building given that anyone with sampling access could simply run the counterfactual.",
  "did": "They chose to build a proxy evaluation with clear ground truth whose questions mirror real use cases, accepting that performance is not directly useful.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating hypothesis generation rather than hypothesis discrimination"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Interpretability tools are most needed where no ground truth exists, so a proxy with checkable answers is the only way to measure reliability; failing on it is a bad sign for harder cases."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:ea22a504e027",
  "problem": "How to interpret why a rank-1 adapter and a single steering vector achieve non-trivial verbalization.",
  "did": "They concluded that IAs elicit a latent self-knowledge capability rather than teaching a new capability.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "teaching models a fundamentally new capability"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Even a rank-1 LoRA adapter and a single steering vector perform reasonably, indicating the behavioral information is already accessible and needs only light elicitation."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:98a62568a87b",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the agents' failures bound the real-world risk of the models.",
  "did": "They explicitly stated the agents are not a robust upper bound on model capability and limited the conclusion to casual users.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The agents they built do not capture the full abilities of the model."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:1fb1577afe9f",
  "problem": "How to obtain large, diverse, correct supervised data of experiments on a subject model.",
  "did": "Scrape science-of-ML arXiv papers for experiment descriptions, have an AI write Python for them, and collect ground truth by executing the code.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Because outputs come from running the code, results stay grounded even if the LM's translation is not faithful to the paper."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:61558b42c52a",
  "problem": "Whether to include unflattering claims about companies that were not strongly supported or central.",
  "did": "They refrained from making unflattering claims that were neither solidly defensible nor relevant to the core assessment, and avoided inviting comparisons between companies.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "inviting salient comparisons between companies on capabilities or safety"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The claims were neither solidly defensible nor particularly relevant to the core assessment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:7e1d2c539d4e",
  "problem": "Which activation tokens to supply as AO input for secret-keeping evaluations, given that token selection affects performance.",
  "did": "They used the full sequence of activations as the default for all secret-keeping evaluations while reporting that single-token or short selections can do better on some tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "single-token inputs on Taboo",
   "shorter selected sequences for Gender"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Simplicity and consistency, and in real auditing without ground-truth labels it is hard to sweep token selection as a hyperparameter."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:6c9217be2719",
  "problem": "How much to trust the headline doubling-time estimate for task horizon, given noise and methodological choices.",
  "did": "METR ran a sensitivity analysis over data noise and methodological choices, reported a range of doubling times rather than a point estimate, and applied a mental correction for eval-friendly tasks being easier than real tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "reporting a single six-month doubling time"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Tasks that make good automatically scorable evals may be systematically easier for models, so absolute horizons may overstate real-world ability, though the exponential trend is solid."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:117aed529f22",
  "problem": "How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.",
  "did": "They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "off-policy false statements",
   "a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability."
 }
]
